Need to search first.I could only cover part of what you asked. My research tools hit their usage limit early, so I couldn't open any full pages. Everything below comes from the search-result text I got back for each page.

- **What's missing:** I found nothing from the Catholic or Orthodox sites, nothing from bibleodyssey.org, and no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. I got only one NET Bible note, quoted on preceptaustin.org. Gill and Ellicott show up only in pieces.
- **Traditions:** none of the pages compared Baptist, Methodist, Reformed or other views on these verses, so I couldn't write that section as asked. Where the commentators disagree with each other, I've marked it **[Differing views]**.
- **Mixed pages:** Bible Hub's "commentaries/1_chronicles/11-1.htm" style pages show several commentators side by side. The excerpts didn't always say who wrote which line, so I name a writer only when the text does.
- **No Shammah or Benaiah details:** for vv. 12–14 and 22–24 I found almost nothing beyond the bare facts.

---

**Overview, vv. 1–9**
- Pastor David Guzik says the elders accepted David for three reasons: he was one of their own people, he had already shown he could lead, and God had plainly called him. He sees these as marks of any leader of God's people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-11/
- The Pulpit Commentary says vv. 1–9 cover the same events as 2 Samuel 5:1–10. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/11.htm
- Constable says Chronicles opens David's story with his crowning over all twelve tribes, probably because the writer cared about the unity of God's people. He also sees these verses as clear proof that God preferred David to Saul. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-11.html

**v. 1**
- Chronicles skips David's seven and a half years ruling Judah alone and Ishbosheth's rival kingdom. The story starts when David rules the whole nation. "All Israel" means the tribes, acting through their elders. (Pulpit) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/11.htm
- Ellicott: the Hebrew word just means "and," so "then" fixes the timing too firmly. Hebron was where the patriarchs were buried and was Judah's capital. "Bone and flesh" is a saying about bodily and then moral unity (Genesis 2:23; Judges 9:2). David was no foreign hero; the tribes loved him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/11-1.htm
- Another commentator on the same page says the phrase shouldn't be pressed to mean blood kinship, since only Judah was David's close family. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/11-1.htm
- Guzik: the phrase matters because David had once lived among the Philistines, and the elders set that aside. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-11/
- Pulpit traces the phrase's history through the Old Testament and says it reaches its highest use in Ephesians 5:30. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/11-1.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik: "led Israel out and brought them in" shows David had already proved he could lead. The shepherd promise showed God's call. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-11/
- One excerpt on Bible Hub says "said unto thee" can mean "said concerning thee." It argues the tribes knew God wanted David as king, so many had been resisting him against their own consciences. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/11-1.htm
- Pulpit says the servant David is given the title the Master claims for himself: the under-shepherd is called what the Chief Shepherd is called (Psalm 23; 1 Peter 5:4). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/11.htm
- Constable: "shepherd" describes David's job, and "ruler" (prince) his office under the LORD. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-11.html
- Bible Hub's chapter study links the shepherd-king language to Psalm 78:70–72, Ezekiel 34:23 and John 10:11. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/1_chronicles/11.htm

**v. 3**
- Matthew Henry: David agreed to protect the people, and they agreed to stay loyal to him. Henry calls this an original contract between ruler and people. Though David could safely have been trusted with absolute power, he took a coronation oath to rule by law. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_011.cfm
- A homily on the Pulpit Homiletics page mentions that some readers call David the first example of a constitutional monarchy. The writer prefers to stress God keeping a promise that had long seemed hopeless. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_chronicles/11.htm
- R. Tuck (same page): David held on to the promise but never forced it to come true. He never built a party for himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_chronicles/11.htm
- Keil and Delitzsch say "according to the word of the LORD by Samuel" was added by the Chronicler to teach, drawing on 1 Samuel 16:13 and 15:28. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/11-1.htm
- Ellicott (on 1 Chr 12:23) says the Hebrew literally reads "according to the mouth" of the LORD: what God spoke through Samuel was really God's own word. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-12.html
- Another excerpt says the public gathering and the repeated anointing were needed for the whole nation to accept the new king. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/11-1.htm
- Constable: God had chosen David long before Saul died, so his crowning was bound to come. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-11.html
- F. Whitfield (Pulpit homilies) reads the people's choosing and anointing of David as a picture of God choosing and anointing Jesus. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-11.html

**vv. 4–5**
- Constable: by fortifying Jerusalem, David gained a secure base on politically neutral ground between Israel and Judah. Taking the city was the foundation for everything that followed, politically and religiously. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-11.html

**v. 6**
- Gill: only Chronicles tells us Joab struck the Jebusites first and so became chief captain, as David had promised. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-chronicles-11.html
- Pulpit takes up an objection: Joab already held high rank, so why offer the post? Its answer is that Joab had fallen out of favour after killing Abner. The open challenge was also a chance for unknown younger men to show what they could do. Winning it secured Joab's place and greatly increased his influence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/11.htm
- Constable: the deed shows Joab was a mighty warrior. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-11.html
- **[Differing views]** R. Tuck (Pulpit homilies) judges Joab harshly overall. He notes Joab went along with David's sin over Bathsheba and later disobeyed him by killing Absalom. Tuck says his influence was bad overall, and he quotes Wordsworth calling Joab the picture of worldly policy and ambition. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-11.html

**vv. 7–8**
- Pulpit links v. 8 with v. 6: Joab "repairing the rest of the city" probably shows him using his new standing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/11.htm
- Gill offers several readings of Joab's work. He may have repaired the walls damaged in the attack. Some render it that he "saved alive" those left in the city. One scholar suggests he became the city's governor, and the Aramaic Targum says "Joab governed the rest of the city." https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-chronicles-11.html

**v. 9**
- Guzik: David was no overnight success. God prepared him over many years, and the real reason for his greatness was that the LORD of hosts was with him. Greatness in God's plan almost always has a hidden price. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-11/
- Constable: God was with David because David was with God, and because God had chosen him as His representative king. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-11.html
- Henry: God worked through people and ordinary means. Drawing strong men to David was itself a sign God was with him. Still, David credited his success to the Lord of hosts, not to his armies. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_011.cfm
- J.R. Thomson (Pulpit homilies): Christians can grow steadily in real goodness by using the means of grace. True progress comes only with God's presence and help. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-11.html
- Bible Hub's chapter study links "the LORD of Hosts was with him" to Joshua 1:5 and Matthew 28:20. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/1_chronicles/11.htm

**v. 10**
- Guzik: David was nothing without his mighty men, and they were nothing without him. Many began as the people in distress, in debt and discontented who joined him at the cave of Adullam (1 Samuel 22:1–2). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-11/
- Henry: much of a great man's strength and honour is borrowed from those who serve him. When God has work to do, He will find or make the people to do it. Those who support the kingdom of the Son of David strengthen themselves. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_011.cfm
- Keil and Delitzsch: "to make him king" covers keeping David on the throne, not just appointing him. That's why the list goes on to record the battles that kept and grew his power. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/11-11.htm
- Ellicott: the phrase means "the chief warriors who showed themselves strong in his support." Lower-ranking warriors are listed in chapter 12. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/11-10.htm
- Pulpit: this list fits better here, at the start of David's reign over all Israel, than where 2 Samuel 23 puts it, after David's last words. The difference suggests both books drew on a common source independently. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/11.htm
- Constable: you learn something about a person from the company they keep. He divides the lists into three groups (11:10–25, 11:26–47, and ch. 12). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-11.html
- Jack Hayford (quoted on preceptaustin) says the list was written down for the exiles back from Babylon, more than 500 years after David. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-11-commentary

**v. 11**
- **The 300 vs. 800 question (2 Samuel 23:8 says 800):**
  - Guzik: probably a copying error. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-11/
  - Benson: Jashobeam killed 300 himself, and others killed 500 more in the pursuit, making 800. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/11-11.htm
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (on the same page) mentions two other proposals. One is two separate battles. The other, from Lightfoot, is that he attacked 800, killed 300, and the rest ran. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/11-11.htm
  - Ellicott thinks the text of Samuel is faulty there. But since Abishai, the lesser hero, killed 300 (v. 20), the larger number may be the right one here. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/11-11.htm
  - Bible Hub's verse commentary: 800 probably describes his wider record, and 300 one particular battle. It adds that God can multiply limited human strength. https://biblehub.com/1_chronicles/11-11.htm
- **"Chief of the captains":** Barnes and Ellicott say the better reading is "chief of the Thirty." Ellicott notes the Hebrew words for "thirty" and "captains" are easily confused, and the original may even have been "head of the Three." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/11-11.htm
- **NET Bible note** (via preceptaustin): the translation follows some Greek manuscripts, "he raised up his spear," rather than the standard Hebrew wording in the parallel verse. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-11-commentary
- **The Targum:** Clarke reports that the Aramaic Targum adds a long praise of David at this verse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/1_chronicles/11.htm

**v. 12**
- Clarke: Jashobeam has already been named as captain of the first group of three, so this verse is about the second, Eleazar. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/11-11.html

**vv. 13–14**
- Keil and Delitzsch: three lines found in 2 Samuel 23:9–11 dropped out here when a copyist's eye skipped, and with them the name of the third hero, Shammah. So the barley-field stand was really Shammah's. The plural verbs in v. 14 should be singular, as in Samuel. A later copyist probably made them plural because he read v. 14 as describing Eleazar and David. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/11-10.htm and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/11-11.htm
- Bible Hub's applied lessons: "the LORD brought about a great victory" shows that with God we can face any challenge. https://biblehub.com/top10/lessons_from_1_chronicles_11.htm

**vv. 15–16**
- Pulpit: neither Samuel nor Chronicles says which three men went. There's no "the" before "three," so we can't assume they are the three just named. Verses 20–25 may point to the second three instead. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/1-chronicles-11.html
- J. Vernon McGee places the episode in the time when David was rejected. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/11-16.html
- Guzik: they had to break through the Philistine garrison and carry the water all the way back to Adullam. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-11/
- R. Tuck cites Robinson's report that there is no spring near Bethlehem. But a cistern about three-quarters of a mile north of the town is called "David's well" by the monks there. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-11.html

**v. 17**
- **[Differing views] Was David wrong to say it?**
  - W. Clarkson (Pulpit homilies) says it was a thoughtless act. A king's wish is likely to be taken as an order, so David should have kept quiet. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-11.html
  - Henry likewise calls what followed "repentance for his own weakness," and says David denied himself a "foolish fancy." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_011.cfm
  - Guzik's notes don't fault him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-11/
- F.B. Meyer (quoted on preceptaustin) applies David's longing to our wish to go back to earlier innocence and joy, and warns that looking back is a mistake. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-11-commentary
- Joseph Parker's sermon on this passage is titled "Longing for the Associations of Childhood." https://biblehub.com/sermons/1_chronicles/11-17.htm

**v. 18**
- Pulpit: pouring it out was a kind of drink offering to God (compare Genesis 35:14; 1 Samuel 7:6). https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/1-chronicles-11.html
- Pulpit Homiletics: David didn't throw the water away or hand it to someone else. Water made sacred by risked human life belonged to God alone. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/1-chronicles-11.html
- Henry: if we have something better than the rest, God, who is the best, should have it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_011.cfm
- **Three readings of the act:**
  - Guzik: it was an act of worship that honoured the men's sacrifice. He quotes a writer who sees three points: it highlights Israelite bravery, it shows David could inspire extraordinary loyalty, and it was recognised as worship. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-11/
  - Clarkson: by pouring it out David rebuked himself and made an offering at the same moment. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-11.html
  - Chuck Smith: David simply felt unworthy to drink it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/1-chronicles-11.html

**v. 19**
- R. Tuck links "the blood of these men" to the law against drinking blood (Leviticus 17:11–12). David treated the water as blood and poured it out as an offering and a thanksgiving that the men survived. https://biblehub.com/sermons/1_chronicles/11-17.htm
- Constable: the episode shows why such men were loyal to David, because he cared unusually about the dangers they faced. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-11.html
- Tuck also says this care for his men's lives tied them more closely to David. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/1-chronicles-11.html
- Henry adds that David showed tenderness toward his servants. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_011.cfm

**vv. 20–21**
- Guzik: Abishai was famous for his fight against 300 men. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-11/
- An excerpt on Bible Hub (writer not named) says vv. 20–25 seem to come from a separate source. Verses 21 and 25 look quoted from a lost poem praising Abishai and Benaiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/11-10.htm
- Preceptaustin's quoted NLT reading makes Abishai commander of the Thirty, though not one of the Three. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-11-commentary

**v. 22**
- Got Questions: Benaiah came from Kabzeel in southern Judah, and his name means "the LORD has built." It sets him apart from another Benaiah, from Pirathon, in the same list (v. 31). https://www.gotquestions.org/Benaiah-in-the-Bible.html
- R. Glover (Pulpit homilies) notes that Benaiah was a priest, son of a high priest, yet a warrior. He reads the lion as a picture of the enemy within, saying we must start by fighting ourselves. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-11.html
- F. Whitfield: those fit to fight the Lord's battles in public are those who first won in secret, like David with the lion and the bear. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-11.html
- Henry: feats like killing the Moabite champions and the Egyptian giant needed God's special presence, as in Joshua 23:10. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_011.cfm
- **Catholic translation:** the Douay-Rheims calls the two Moabites "the two ariels of Moab," shown on Bible Hub's Catholic page. https://biblehub.com/catholic/1_chronicles/11-22.htm

**vv. 23–24**
- Clarke points readers to his note on 2 Samuel 23:21 for the Egyptian episode. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/1_chronicles/11.htm
- Got Questions sums Benaiah up as a man who outwitted the Egyptian giant and killed him with his own spear. It also says David put him over "the thirty" (1 Chronicles 27:6). https://www.gotquestions.org/Benaiah-in-the-Bible.html

Once my tools are available again, the next pages to read in full would be the complete Ellicott and Gill chapter pages, the NET Bible notes, and the Catholic and Orthodox sites.
